question: Does turning up the music in a bar cause people to drink more beer?
outcome: Beer consumption per patron: number of glasses ordered and mean time to drink a glass, under high-volume (88 dB) vs normal (72 dB) bar music.
citation: Gueguen, N., Jacob, C., Le Guellec, H., Morineau, T., & Lourel, M. (2008), 'Sound level of environmental music and drinking behavior: A field experiment with beer drinkers', Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research, 32(10), 1795-1798. DOI 10.1111/j.1530-0277.2008.00764.x.
design: Naturalistic field experiment: 40 male beer drinkers (18-25) observed in 2 bars in western France over 3 Saturday nights; music volume randomly set to 72 dB (normal) or 88 dB (high).

dataset.note: Lock5 3e ships no dataset for this question (checked lock5stat.com/datapage3e.html; only 'beer' match is PumpkinBeer). CSV is a documented reconstruction of per-patron data from the published group means (2.6 vs 3.4 glasses; 14.51 vs 11.45 min per glass, via the paper abstract and Reuters/HealthDay/Daily Star coverage); balanced 20/20 assignment assumed; per-patron spread is a documented assumption -- provenance in the CSV header.

conclusion: With random assignment of patrons to sound levels, the experiment supports a causal conclusion: louder music made patrons drink more and faster. Mean glasses ordered rose from 2.6 (72 dB) to 3.4 (88 dB), diff +0.8 (95% bootstrap CI +0.30 to +1.30; Welch t=2.97, p=5.17e-03); mean time per glass fell from 14.51 to 11.45 min, diff -3.06 min (95% bootstrap CI -4.26 to -1.89; Welch t=-4.91, p=2.49e-05). Randomization tests (100k label permutations) agree. Caveats: young male patrons in 2 French bars only; reconstructed spread assumed (documented).
